screens.title: Advanced Serialization: Custom Encoders, Decoders, and dataclasses
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a practical, production-ready understanding of advanced JSON serialization in Python. You will learn how to extend the standard json module so that custom class instances and datetime objects can be converted to JSON and then reconstructed safely. We'll use two complementary tools: a custom JSONEncoder or a default function to control how problematic objects are turned into serializable forms, and an object_hook to rehydrate dictionaries back into class instances. You'll also see how dataclasses pair with dataclasses. asdict() to simplify conversion, and how to handle nested dataclasses and lists while preserving datetime accuracy. Along the way we'll note common mistakes — for example, assuming object_hook will convert plain strings back into datetimes — and safer patterns such as tagging objects and validating input during deserialization. By the end, you'll be able to serialize complex object graphs for network interchange or persistent storage and then rebuild the original Python structures without losing type information or corrupting relationships. Keep an eye on the code examples: they show both encoder subclasses and minimal default functions, plus hands-on dataclass patterns you'll reuse immediately.

Each objective includes practical code work so you can apply these skills in real projects and tests.

screens.title: Why json.dumps fails on custom objects
screens.narratorSegment: When you call the json module's dumps function on a dictionary that contains a custom class instance or a datetime, Python raises a TypeError because the default encoder only knows how to serialize basic built-in types like dict, list, str, int, float, bool, and None. That error is not a bug in your object; it is a clear signal that you must provide instructions for how to convert the object into a JSON-serializable representation. A practical example is trying to dump a Point instance or a datetime object directly. The right mental model is that JSON encoders must work with primitive structures: strings, numbers, lists and plain dictionaries. Anything else requires translation. A common misconception is to try and rely on str conversions everywhere; while coercing everything to strings will avoid errors, it destroys type information and makes deserialization ambiguous. Instead, we tag objects or convert datetimes to ISO strings so the structure and intent remain clear. In short, TypeError tells you to implement a conversion path: either supply a custom JSONEncoder subclass, pass a default() function, or preconvert objects to dicts and strings before calling dumps. Which approach you choose depends on reuse, code locality, and how many types you must support.

content.html:
Core Concept › Chapter 7.8 › TypeError: Not JSON serializable
What triggers the error
An object outside json's built-in primitives ends up in the structure passed to dumps.
Concrete example
from datetime import datetime
import json

class Point:
  def __init__(self, x, y):
    self.x = x
    self.y = y

p = Point(1, 2)
# This will raise TypeError: Object of type Point is not JSON serializable
json.dumps({'point': p})
Why stringifying is a bad habit
  • It discards type information and makes deserialization ambiguous.
  • Dates turned into strings may lose timezone or format assumptions.
  • It hides structure that your object_hook could use to reinstantiate objects properly.
Alternatives to stringification
Custom JSONEncoder
Subclass JSONEncoder and override default() to return dicts, lists or strings intentionally.
Default function
Pass a single function to json.dumps for small projects to map unknown types to serializable forms.
Pre-conversion
Convert dataclasses via asdict and datetimes via isoformat before dumping for explicit control.
Key Takeaway

Treat TypeError as a prompt to provide a clear, reversible translation for each non-primitive object you want in JSON.

screens.title: Custom JSONEncoder: subclass and default()
screens.narratorSegment: A JSONEncoder subclass gives you a centralized place to define serialization rules that apply whenever you call json. dumps with cls set. The key method to override is default, which receives any object the encoder cannot handle. Inside default you check types and return a JSON-serializable form. A common pattern is to return a dictionary with a unique tag key such as 'Point' or 'Project' and the object's attributes. For datetime objects return the ISO formatted string. If the type is unknown, delegate to the parent default to raise TypeError. This approach cleanly separates serialization logic from your domain classes and is reusable across the codebase. As an example, the supplied CustomEncoder handles Point and datetime; ProjectEncoder uses dataclasses. asdict to convert dataclass instances then tags the dict so object_hook can spot it on load. A typical misconception is to mutate the original object during default; default should always return an independent serializable value. Finally, remember that passing a default function to json. dumps is an acceptable alternative for small projects: it's a function that receives the object and returns a serializable value or raises TypeError, but lacks the inheritance structure of a subclass.

keyIdea.text: Override default(), return tagged dictionaries or ISO strings, and delegate unknowns to the base class for proper errors.

content.html:
Process Flow › Custom JSONEncoder
Encoder subclass walkthrough
Centralize serialization in a reusable class.
import json
from datetime import datetime

class Point:
  def __init__(self, x, y):
    self.x = x
    self.y = y

class CustomEncoder(json.JSONEncoder):
  def default(self, obj):
    if isinstance(obj, Point):
      return {'__Point__': True, 'x': obj.x, 'y': obj.y}
    if isinstance(obj, datetime):
      return obj.isoformat()
    return super().default(obj)

p = Point(10, 20)
json_string = json.dumps({'point': p, 'time': datetime.now()}, cls=CustomEncoder, indent=2)
print(json_string)
Notes
  • Tagging with a unique key makes object_hook detection easy on load.
  • Returning dicts preserves attribute structure for reconstruction.
  • Use isoformat for datetime to preserve precision and a standard format.
Supporting blocks
Example
Using cls=CustomEncoder in json.dumps serializes Point objects and datetimes as intended.
Common mistake
Mutating the original object inside default or returning non-serializable values causes subtle bugs.
Key Takeaway

Use encoder subclasses when you need reusable, centralized serialization rules across your application.

screens.title: Alternative: default function for json.dumps
screens.narratorSegment: For small scripts or when you only need to handle one or two types, passing a default function to json. dumps is a compact alternative to subclassing JSONEncoder. The default function is called with the object the encoder cannot serialize and must return a serializable representation or raise TypeError. This is convenient because it avoids creating a new class and is easy to inline near the call site. In practice, you'll still follow the same pattern: check isinstance for known types, return a tagged dict for custom classes, and return isoformat for datetimes. The tradeoff is that you lose the object-oriented reuse benefits of a subclass and you cannot attach state to the encoder as easily. Also, overusing default=str is brittle: converting arbitrary objects to strings removes structure and makes deserialization unreliable. Use default functions when the handling is narrow and local; prefer encoder subclasses for broader reuse. A simple example provided in the chapter shows how to implement custom_default_func for Point and datetime and pass it to json. dumps. Remember to return the same tag conventions so your object_hook can rely on them during deserialization.

Definition › default function
default function example
Lightweight inline mapping for a couple of types.
def custom_default_func(obj):
  if isinstance(obj, Point):
    return {'__Point__': True, 'x': obj.x, 'y': obj.y}
  elif isinstance(obj, datetime):
    return obj.isoformat()
  raise TypeError(f"Object of type {obj.__class__.__name__} is not JSON serializable")

json_string = json.dumps(data_to_serialize, default=custom_default_func, indent=2)
  • Keep the function focused; avoid handling too many types here.
  • Maintain consistent tagging so deserialization remains straightforward.
Tradeoffs
Pro
Simple, minimal code change for local serialization needs.
Con
Less reusable and harder to maintain if you support many types across the codebase.
Key Takeaway

Use default functions for targeted, local problems; upgrade to a subclass when rules must be shared.

screens.title: object_hook: reconstructing custom types
screens.narratorSegment: Deserialization with json. loads gives you a place to reconstitute your original Python objects via the object_hook parameter. This hook is a function called with every dictionary that json constructs during parsing. Inside the hook you check for your tag keys — for example, 'Point' — and then create and return an instance of the appropriate class, often using the values stored in the dictionary. Important detail: object_hook only sees dictionaries. If you serialized a datetime as a string, object_hook will not automatically be called for that string. That means you either need to serialize datetimes as tagged dictionaries, perform a post-processing pass to convert timestamp strings back to datetime objects, or ensure your object_hook knows the structure around the string and can convert it when the string is part of a dict. Another common pitfall is assuming order of hook calls; nested dictionaries are passed to object_hook bottom-up, so inner objects may be converted before the outer container is processed. Design your tags and reconstruction logic accordingly. Also validate incoming data; only instantiate classes you expect to avoid unsafe behavior when handling untrusted JSON.

keyIdea.title: object_hook behavior
keyIdea.text: object_hook processes dictionaries bottom-up; it won't see plain strings — design tagging and post-processing for datetimes accordingly.

content.html:
Process Flow › object_hook
object_hook example
def custom_object_hook(dct):
  if '__Point__' in dct:
    return Point(dct['x'], dct['y'])
  return dct

loaded = json.loads(json_string, object_hook=custom_object_hook)
# loaded['point_instance'] will be a Point instance
  • Hook receives each dict; return an instance to replace that dict in the result.
  • For nested objects the hook runs on inner dicts before outer ones; plan accordingly.
  • Strings representing datetimes remain strings unless you convert them explicitly.
Guidance and warnings
Bottom-up order
Inner dictionaries are passed to object_hook first, which can help when nesting objects like tasks inside projects.
Security
Only reconstruct known safe types and validate fields to avoid creating unsafe objects from untrusted JSON.
Key Takeaway

Use object_hook to detect tags and reconstruct objects, and handle datetimes separately since they deserialize as strings.

screens.title: Handling datetime: serialize to ISO, convert on load
screens.narratorSegment: Datetime objects are not dictionaries, so the default JSON encoder turns them into TypeError unless you provide a conversion. A consistent and interoperable pattern is to convert datetimes to ISO 8601 strings using the object's isoformat method during serialization. This preserves precision and is widely parseable. On deserialization you need to convert those ISO strings back into datetime objects. Remember the object_hook only receives dictionaries, so timestamp strings that were serialized as bare strings will not be converted inside object_hook. You have two safe choices: serialize datetimes as tagged dictionaries so the object_hook can reconstruct them, or perform a second pass after json. loads to walk the structure and convert any ISO-like timestamp strings you expect. A common misconception is to assume object_hook will see and convert every value; it only sees dicts. In nested dataclasses, ensure the encoder converted inner datetime fields into ISO strings or tagged dicts so the reconstructing logic can find and reparse them. Finally, validate the parsed string with fromisoformat or a safe parser and handle ValueError to avoid accepting malformed data from untrusted sources.

content.html:
Architecture › Datetime handling
ISO serialization and explicit conversion
Choose tagged dicts or a post-load pass to rehydrate datetime strings.
# serialization (in encoder)
if isinstance(obj, datetime):
  return obj.isoformat()

# deserialization (post-load)
if isinstance(loaded['timestamp'], str):
  loaded['timestamp'] = datetime.fromisoformat(loaded['timestamp'])
  • ISO strings are portable and precise; prefer them over custom string formats.
  • object_hook won't touch bare strings; plan for explicit conversion.
  • Always catch parsing exceptions when converting untrusted input.
Example options
Tagged datetime
Return {'__datetime__': True, 'value': iso_string} so the hook can reparse it.
Second pass
After json.loads, walk the structure and convert known timestamp fields using fromisoformat.
Key Takeaway

Design a clear rule for datetimes; convert and validate explicitly on load rather than assuming automatic conversion.

screens.title: dataclasses.asdict() and reconstructing dataclasses
screens.narratorSegment: Dataclasses are commonly used as simple data containers and are ideal for serialization because the dataclasses module provides a helper, asdict, which recursively converts a dataclass instance into plain Python dictionaries and lists. That means after asdict you have a structure json can handle, provided all leaf values are serializable — for example, convert nested datetimes to ISO strings first. On load, you take the parsed dictionary and unpack it into the dataclass constructor using ClassName(loaded_dict). For nested dataclasses or lists of dataclasses, apply reconstruction recursively: ensure nested task dictionaries are converted into Task instances before constructing the outer Project. The example in the chapter shows converting a Product dataclass: call asdict, change last_updated to isoformat, dump to JSON, load back to dict, convert the timestamp using fromisoformat, and then call Product(loaded_product_dict). A misconception is assuming asdict will automatically convert datetimes; it will not. asdict only converts dataclass fields into plain dict structure. You still must handle non-standard types yourself. The pattern of asdict plus explicit handling for non-primitives keeps your serialization logic explicit and easy to maintain. dataclasses.asdict() and reconstructing dataclasses means use asdict to prepare dataclasses for json, then reconstruct by unpacking dictionaries and converting non-primitive fields first.. In practical terms, serialize dataclasses to dicts and rebuild them with classname(**loaded_dict). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dataclass round-trip
keyIdea.text: Use asdict to prepare dataclasses for JSON, then reconstruct by unpacking dictionaries and converting non-primitive fields first.

content.html:
Definition › dataclasses.asdict()
dataclass serialization pattern
Convert to dict, handle non-primitives, then dump.
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from datetime import datetime
import json

@dataclass
class Product:
  id: int
  name: str
  price: float
  last_updated: datetime

p = Product(101, 'Mouse', 25.99, datetime.now())
product_dict = asdict(p)
product_dict['last_updated'] = product_dict['last_updated'].isoformat()
json_product = json.dumps(product_dict, indent=2)

# On load
loaded = json.loads(json_product)
loaded['last_updated'] = datetime.fromisoformat(loaded['last_updated'])
product = Product(**loaded)
  • asdict is recursive: nested dataclasses become nested dicts and lists.
  • Handle non-standard leaves (datetime, custom classes) explicitly before dumping.
Hints
Nested dataclasses
Reconstruct inner dataclasses first so outer constructors receive instances, not dicts.
Validation
Validate fields before passing to constructors to avoid runtime errors.
Key Takeaway

asdict simplifies the path to JSON but you must still handle leaf types that aren't JSON-native.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on pattern
keyIdea.text: Tag dataclass dicts in the encoder and reconstruct them safely in object_hook, handling nested conversions and datetime parsing defensively.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Project & Task example
ProjectEncoder and project_object_hook
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from datetime import datetime
import json

@dataclass
class Task:
  id: int
  description: str
  due_date: datetime
  completed: bool = False

@dataclass
class Project:
  id: int
  name: str
  start_date: datetime
  tasks: list[Task]

# Encoder
class ProjectEncoder(json.JSONEncoder):
  def default(self, obj):
    if isinstance(obj, datetime):
      return obj.isoformat()
    if isinstance(obj, (Project, Task)):
      data = asdict(obj)
      # convert datetimes in the dict
      for k, v in data.items():
        if isinstance(v, datetime):
          data[k] = v.isoformat()
        if isinstance(v, list):
          data[k] = [asdict(item) for item in v]
      data[f'__{obj.__class__.__name__}__'] = True
      return data
    return super().default(obj)

# ... (serialization and hook shown on next panel)
Notes and verification
Hook behavior
When Task dicts are tagged they become Task instances before the Project hook runs.
Defensive parsing
Wrap datetime.fromisoformat in try/except to avoid exceptions on malformed data.
Key Takeaway

Tag-and-hook with asdict is a clear, testable approach for nested dataclasses with timestamps.

screens.title: Object graph strategies: nested objects vs. IDs
screens.narratorSegment: When your model includes objects that reference each other — an object graph — you must choose how to represent those relationships in JSON. Two common strategies are nested objects and reference by ID. Nested objects are simple and intuitive: the parent contains full child objects inline, which maps cleanly to dataclasses. asdict. This is ideal when the nested objects are tightly coupled and the entire graph is transferred together. However, nested structures can be inefficient or create duplication when many parents reference the same child. The alternative is to represent relationships by ID: serialize each object once, assign stable IDs, and reference those IDs from other objects. This reduces duplication and mirrors relational storage, but it requires additional logic on deserialization to resolve IDs back to object references and can complicate round-trips. A common misconception is to always nest because it's simpler; in larger systems, use IDs for shared resources and nested representations for contained objects. For JSON-based APIs choose the method that best balances size, clarity, and reconstruction complexity, and document your tags and ID resolution behavior so consumers can implement corresponding object_hook logic safely.

content.html:
Comparison › Nested vs ID references
Nested objects
Simple round-trips, best for owned children.
  • Easy to implement with asdict and object_hook.
  • Can duplicate data when children are shared across parents.
  • Good for small graphs transferred as a single payload.
ID references
Avoid duplication; resolve IDs on load.
  • Serializes each entity once and references by stable IDs.
  • Requires a resolution step on deserialization to map IDs to instances.
  • Better for shared resources or large graphs.
Design rule
Choose nesting for ownership and small payloads; choose IDs when sharing and duplication become problems, and design hooks or a resolver to map IDs back to objects on load.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing custom deserialization, a few common mistakes recur. First, blindly instantiating classes based on string names contained in JSON is dangerous: it can allow attackers to trick your code into creating unexpected objects. Always limit reconstruction to known safe types and validate field values before calling constructors. Second, assuming object_hook converts bare strings into rich types is incorrect; object_hook only handles dictionaries. Convert plain timestamp strings with a second pass or tag them at serialization time. Third, returning non-serializable values from default or default functions will reintroduce TypeError; always return primitives, dicts, or lists. Fourth, mutating input data structures during serialization or deserialization can produce subtle bugs; prefer returning new dicts or new instances. Finally, avoid using default=str as a catch-all: it makes deserialization lossy and undermines type safety. The secure practice is explicit tagging, validation, and mapping only of expected, documented types. Add unit tests that assert type recovery and timestamp conversion behavior to detect regressions early. In practical terms, avoid insecure instantiation and brittle conversions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a practical, production-ready understanding of advanced JSON serialization in Python. You will learn how to extend the standard json module so that custom class instances and datetime objects can be converted to JSON and then reconstructed safely. We'll use two complementary tools: a custom JSONEncoder or a default function to control how problematic objects are turned into serializable forms, and an object_hook to rehydrate dictionaries back into class instances. You'll also see how dataclasses pair with dataclasses. asdict() to simplify conversion, and how to handle nested dataclasses and lists while preserving datetime accuracy. Along the way we'll note common mistakes — for example, assuming object_hook will convert plain strings back into datetimes — and safer patterns such as tagging objects and validating input during deserialization. By the end, you'll be able to serialize complex object graphs for network interchange or persistent storage and then rebuild the original Python structures without losing type information or corrupting relationships. Keep an eye on the code examples: they show both encoder subclasses and minimal default functions, plus hands-on dataclass patterns you'll reuse immediately.

These objectives guide our coding practice and assessments. First, you'll develop custom JSONEncoder subclasses to serialize types that the default json encoder cannot handle, such as instances of user-defined classes and datetime objects. You'll practice writing a default method that returns a serializable representation and learn when to delegate to the base class. Second, you'll implement object_hook functions for json. loads to detect tagged dictionaries and reconstruct Python objects; you will learn how object_hook is called for each decoded dictionary and why plain strings need separate handling. Third, we'll show how to serialize and deserialize dataclasses efficiently using dataclasses. asdict and then unpack the dictionary into the dataclass constructor, including handling nested dataclasses and lists. Finally, you'll recognize common pitfalls — for example, assuming object_hook converts datetime strings automatically — and adopt best practices such as tagging, validating input during deserialization, and choosing IDs versus nested objects for complex graphs. Each objective includes practical code work so you can apply these skills in real projects and tests.

This second objectives slide turns goals into small practice tasks. You will begin by provoking the TypeError that json. dumps raises when it meets an unknown object type so you understand the failure mode. Next you'll write a JSONEncoder subclass and override default to return either a tagged dictionary for your class or an ISO string for datetimes; test this on a Point instance and a timestamp. Then practice writing a minimal default function that json. dumps can accept for small projects. For deserialization, you'll implement an object_hook that checks for tags and reconstructs Point objects and, for dataclasses, converts nested dictionaries into dataclass instances. Finally, apply the pattern to the Project and Task dataclasses: serialize using asdict and ProjectEncoder, then load with project_object_hook, converting ISO strings back to datetimes and nested tasks back to Task instances. Each task ends with a quick verification step: assert the reconstructed types are the expected classes and that timestamp fields are datetime objects.

When you call the json module's dumps function on a dictionary that contains a custom class instance or a datetime, Python raises a TypeError because the default encoder only knows how to serialize basic built-in types like dict, list, str, int, float, bool, and None. That error is not a bug in your object; it is a clear signal that you must provide instructions for how to convert the object into a JSON-serializable representation. A practical example is trying to dump a Point instance or a datetime object directly. The right mental model is that JSON encoders must work with primitive structures: strings, numbers, lists and plain dictionaries. Anything else requires translation. A common misconception is to try and rely on str conversions everywhere; while coercing everything to strings will avoid errors, it destroys type information and makes deserialization ambiguous. Instead, we tag objects or convert datetimes to ISO strings so the structure and intent remain clear. In short, TypeError tells you to implement a conversion path: either supply a custom JSONEncoder subclass, pass a default() function, or preconvert objects to dicts and strings before calling dumps. Which approach you choose depends on reuse, code locality, and how many types you must support.

A JSONEncoder subclass gives you a centralized place to define serialization rules that apply whenever you call json. dumps with cls set. The key method to override is default, which receives any object the encoder cannot handle. Inside default you check types and return a JSON-serializable form. A common pattern is to return a dictionary with a unique tag key such as 'Point' or 'Project' and the object's attributes. For datetime objects return the ISO formatted string. If the type is unknown, delegate to the parent default to raise TypeError. This approach cleanly separates serialization logic from your domain classes and is reusable across the codebase. As an example, the supplied CustomEncoder handles Point and datetime; ProjectEncoder uses dataclasses. asdict to convert dataclass instances then tags the dict so object_hook can spot it on load. A typical misconception is to mutate the original object during default; default should always return an independent serializable value. Finally, remember that passing a default function to json. dumps is an acceptable alternative for small projects: it's a function that receives the object and returns a serializable value or raises TypeError, but lacks the inheritance structure of a subclass.

For small scripts or when you only need to handle one or two types, passing a default function to json. dumps is a compact alternative to subclassing JSONEncoder. The default function is called with the object the encoder cannot serialize and must return a serializable representation or raise TypeError. This is convenient because it avoids creating a new class and is easy to inline near the call site. In practice, you'll still follow the same pattern: check isinstance for known types, return a tagged dict for custom classes, and return isoformat for datetimes. The tradeoff is that you lose the object-oriented reuse benefits of a subclass and you cannot attach state to the encoder as easily. Also, overusing default=str is brittle: converting arbitrary objects to strings removes structure and makes deserialization unreliable. Use default functions when the handling is narrow and local; prefer encoder subclasses for broader reuse. A simple example provided in the chapter shows how to implement custom_default_func for Point and datetime and pass it to json. dumps. Remember to return the same tag conventions so your object_hook can rely on them during deserialization.

Deserialization with json. loads gives you a place to reconstitute your original Python objects via the object_hook parameter. This hook is a function called with every dictionary that json constructs during parsing. Inside the hook you check for your tag keys — for example, 'Point' — and then create and return an instance of the appropriate class, often using the values stored in the dictionary. Important detail: object_hook only sees dictionaries. If you serialized a datetime as a string, object_hook will not automatically be called for that string. That means you either need to serialize datetimes as tagged dictionaries, perform a post-processing pass to convert timestamp strings back to datetime objects, or ensure your object_hook knows the structure around the string and can convert it when the string is part of a dict. Another common pitfall is assuming order of hook calls; nested dictionaries are passed to object_hook bottom-up, so inner objects may be converted before the outer container is processed. Design your tags and reconstruction logic accordingly. Also validate incoming data; only instantiate classes you expect to avoid unsafe behavior when handling untrusted JSON.

Datetime objects are not dictionaries, so the default JSON encoder turns them into TypeError unless you provide a conversion. A consistent and interoperable pattern is to convert datetimes to ISO 8601 strings using the object's isoformat method during serialization. This preserves precision and is widely parseable. On deserialization you need to convert those ISO strings back into datetime objects. Remember the object_hook only receives dictionaries, so timestamp strings that were serialized as bare strings will not be converted inside object_hook. You have two safe choices: serialize datetimes as tagged dictionaries so the object_hook can reconstruct them, or perform a second pass after json. loads to walk the structure and convert any ISO-like timestamp strings you expect. A common misconception is to assume object_hook will see and convert every value; it only sees dicts. In nested dataclasses, ensure the encoder converted inner datetime fields into ISO strings or tagged dicts so the reconstructing logic can find and reparse them. Finally, validate the parsed string with fromisoformat or a safe parser and handle ValueError to avoid accepting malformed data from untrusted sources.

Dataclasses are commonly used as simple data containers and are ideal for serialization because the dataclasses module provides a helper, asdict, which recursively converts a dataclass instance into plain Python dictionaries and lists. When your model includes objects that reference each other — an object graph — you must choose how to represent those relationships in JSON. Two common strategies are nested objects and reference by ID. Nested objects are simple and intuitive: the parent contains full child objects inline, which maps cleanly to dataclasses. asdict. This is ideal when the nested objects are tightly coupled and the entire graph is transferred together. However, nested structures can be inefficient or create duplication when many parents reference the same child. The alternative is to represent relationships by ID: serialize each object once, assign stable IDs, and reference those IDs from other objects. This reduces duplication and mirrors relational storage, but it requires additional logic on deserialization to resolve IDs back to object references and can complicate round-trips. A common misconception is to always nest because it's simpler; in larger systems, use IDs for shared resources and nested representations for contained objects. For JSON-based APIs choose the method that best balances size, clarity, and reconstruction complexity, and document your tags and ID resolution behavior so consumers can implement corresponding object_hook logic safely.
